strengths: Novel reframing of CLIP-based facial expression recognition using structured Action Unit (AU) textual prompts rather than generic class prompts or LLM-generated descriptions, providing an interpretable and lightweight alternative to full CLIP fine-tuning.

The proposed CLIP-AUTT test-time personalization module (entropy-guided temporal window selection + AU prompt tuning) is well-motivated for the specific challenge of subtle, subject-specific expressions, and is conceptually distinct from prior image-level CLIP TTA methods (TPT, TDA, DPE, PromptAlign, ReTA).

Extensive empirical evaluation across three distinct and challenging datasets (BioVid, StressID, BAH) with numerous strong, recent baselines from both CLIP-FER and CLIP-TTA literature, plus an adapted video-level TTA baseline (T3AL).

Rich set of ablations (temporal module design choice, AU vs. class-prompt vs. fusion, window length sensitivity, robustness to number of target subjects, AU adapter effect via t-SNE) that support the design decisions.

Qualitative cross-validation of predicted AU activations against an independent AU detector (OpenFace), which adds some external validity to the claim that the model learns semantically meaningful AU patterns despite lacking AU ground truth.
Efficiency analysis (throughput, parameters, GFLOPs) indicates the method is lightweight relative to full fine-tuning approaches, supporting practical applicability.
weaknesses: The 46-item 'AU' vocabulary conflates true FACS Action Units with head-pose/gaze/tongue/lip-bite descriptors (e.g., head turn left/right, eyes look up/down, lick lips, tongue show), which are not part of the standard FACS AU taxonomy; this undermines the paper's central claim of grounding prompts in interpretable, anatomically-defined AUs and could be seen as a terminology overclaim.

No quantitative validation against AU ground truth or detector outputs is provided — only a handful of qualitative examples compare predicted AUs to OpenFace detections; the claim that the model 'captures AU semantics' rests primarily on downstream classification accuracy rather than direct AU-level evidence.

On the BAH dataset, UAR for CLIP-AUTT (50.2%) and nearly all baselines hovers at chance level despite improved WAR/F1, suggesting the model largely predicts the majority class and does not meaningfully solve the harder, class-imbalanced ambivalence recognition problem, which tempers the 'robust personalization' claims for this dataset.

Personalization evaluation uses only 10 target subjects per dataset, and subject-wise results (e.g., Table 2) show large variance (WAR ranging from 50 to 100 across subjects), raising concerns about the statistical robustness and generalizability of the reported average gains; no variance/standard deviation across multiple runs or seeds is reported anywhere in the paper.

TTA baselines (TPT, TDA, DPE, PromptAlign, ReTA) were originally designed for static image classification and are adapted to this video setting without full evidence that they were properly re-tuned/optimized for fair comparison, which could bias the comparison in favor of the proposed video-specific method.

Entropy minimization for AU prompt tuning is performed directly on the same test video subsequently used for prediction (single-sample, no separate held-out adaptation data), which is standard in TTA but the paper does not discuss potential overfitting/self-confirmation risks in this specific unsupervised personalization setting.

The exact number and definition of expression classes per dataset (e.g., binary pain/no-pain vs. multi-level) is not clearly specified in the main text, making it harder to fully interpret WAR/F1 results and compare against related work in the field.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea of replacing generic class prompts or LLM-generated captions with structured Action Unit (AU) text prompts within CLIP, providing an interpretable and anatomically grounded semantic space for fine-grained/subtle expression recognition, without requiring AU ground-truth labels.

Two coherent contributions (CLIP-AU for pretraining and CLIP-AUTT for test-time personalization) that build logically on one another and address a clearly articulated gap: subject-specific variability in subtle expressions.

The entropy-guided temporal window selection strategy for CLIP-AUTT is a sensible, lightweight mechanism to focus test-time adaptation on the most expressive/reliable segment of a video, which is intuitively appropriate for gradually emerging subtle expressions.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three challenging and diverse video ER datasets (BioVid, StressID, BAH), with comparisons against multiple recent CLIP-based FER methods and six TTA baselines (image-level and video-level), showing consistent improvements in WAR and especially F1.

Thorough ablation studies (temporal module design, AU vs. class-prompt ablations, AU adapter t-SNE visualization, window-length sensitivity, CP+AU fusion) that support the design choices and improve interpretability of the method.

Qualitative validation using an independent AU detector (OpenFace) to cross-check the plausibility of the AU activations predicted by the model, partially compensating for the lack of AU ground truth.
Subject-wise result tables (in main text and supplementary) provide transparency about performance variance across individuals, which is valuable for a personalization-focused method.
Code is stated to be released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The AU semantics are never validated quantitatively against any ground-truth AU annotations; the OpenFace-based qualitative comparison covers only a handful of examples and could be strengthened with a systematic quantitative agreement analysis (e.g., correlation or IoU of top-activated AUs vs. OpenFace outputs) across the test set.

On the BAH dataset, UAR values for CLIP-AUTT and most baselines are close to chance level (~50%) despite reasonable WAR, suggesting the model may be exploiting class imbalance rather than genuinely discriminating expressions in this harder, in-the-wild setting; this limitation is not explicitly discussed or analyzed in the main text.

The list of 46 AUs and their textual descriptions appears to be manually curated by the authors rather than derived from a standard, verifiable FACS-coder-validated set; the provenance and validity of these specific AU-to-text mappings could be better justified or cited.

Because CLIP-AUTT operates at the video/window level with sliding-window temporal aggregation while most TTA baselines are single-image methods, part of the reported gain could stem simply from temporal aggregation/window selection rather than the AU-prompt-tuning mechanism itself; an ablation isolating the entropy-window-selection contribution from the AU-prompt-tuning contribution (beyond the coarse CP-vs-AU ablation) would strengthen the causal claims.

Personalization is evaluated on a fairly small number of target subjects (10 per dataset), consistent with prior work protocols but still limiting the statistical robustness of subject-wise conclusions.

Limited discussion of computational/latency overhead of per-subject test-time optimization (10 iterations per video, sliding window over frames) in scenarios requiring real-time deployment, despite an efficiency figure being presented.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem: subject-specific personalization for subtle, fine-grained facial expressions (pain, stress, ambivalence), which is under-served by prototypical CLIP-based FER methods relying on class prompts or LLM descriptions.

Uses AU semantics as structured, interpretable text prompts instead of noisy LLM-generated descriptions, providing an efficient, lightweight (adapter-only) alternative to full CLIP fine-tuning, with favorable efficiency/throughput/GFLOPs trade-offs shown in Fig. 1(d).

Combines entropy-guided temporal window selection with unsupervised AU prompt tuning at test time in a coherent, unsupervised pipeline that requires no AU ground-truth labels or subject-level supervision.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three distinct and challenging datasets (BioVid, StressID, BAH) with comparisons against multiple recent CLIP-based FER and CLIP-based/video TTA baselines (TPT, TDA, DPE, PromptAlign, ReTA, T3AL), showing consistent gains, especially in F1 under class imbalance.

Thorough ablation studies (temporal module design choice with logit/statistics analysis, window length sensitivity, prompt template selection, AU-vs-class-prompt comparisons, early/late fusion, AU adapter impact via t-SNE, robustness across seeds, sampling rate, additional FERV39K dataset, phrase vs sentence-level prompts) demonstrate a careful and comprehensive experimental protocol in the supplementary material.
Qualitative validation of predicted AUs against an external AU detector (OpenFace) provides some evidence that the learned AU activations are semantically meaningful rather than arbitrary.
Individual component analysis (Table 5) cleanly isolates the respective contributions of window selection and AU prompt tuning.
weaknesses: Several core building blocks (entropy minimization for TTA, prompt tuning, sliding-window temporal segmentation) are adapted from existing techniques (TPT, PromptAlign, T3AL); the novelty largely lies in their combination and application to AU-guided personalization rather than fundamentally new methodology.

In the subject-wise BioVid results (Table 2 / supplementary Table 2), UAR values are reported as numerically identical to WAR for every method and every subject, which is suspicious and raises questions about whether UAR was computed correctly or is a redundant/erroneous duplication of WAR; this undermines confidence in some reported numbers.

On the most realistic and challenging dataset (BAH), gains are comparatively modest, and UAR for CLIP-AUTT and most baselines is essentially at chance (~50%), suggesting limited robustness in naturalistic, less-controlled settings; while the paper acknowledges this as a limitation, it somewhat weakens the generality of the claimed contribution.

Personalization is evaluated on only 10 target subjects per dataset, and formal statistical significance/variance analysis is provided only for StressID (3 seeds); the robustness of subject-wise gains elsewhere is not rigorously quantified.

The fixed vocabulary of 46 AUs is applied uniformly across pain (BioVid), stress (StressID), and ambivalence (BAH) tasks without discussion of whether this generic AU set is optimal for each distinct expression domain, leaving open questions about sensitivity to AU prompt selection/design.

Because CLIP-AU itself is pretrained (with adapter and classifier) using labeled source-subject data before CLIP-AUTT's test-time stage, claims of avoiding "CLIP fine-tuning" refer only to the frozen backbone; the overall pipeline still depends on supervised source training, which should be stated more explicitly when comparing efficiency/simplicity against fully fine-tuned baselines.

Selecting only a single low-entropy temporal window for adaptation risks discarding potentially useful complementary information from the rest of the video; no ablation compares against aggregating multiple confident windows.

The writing, while detailed, is dense with heavy notation reuse (e.g., z_sm vs z'_sm, s_i used for both AU similarity vectors and entropy indices) that could hinder reproducibility and readability without careful cross-referencing.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea of replacing generic class-level or LLM-generated text prompts with structured, interpretable Action Unit (AU) descriptions within CLIP for fine-grained facial expression recognition, addressing a genuine limitation of existing CLIP-FER methods.

Clean two-stage framework: CLIP-AU for AU-guided fine-grained alignment (avoiding costly fine-tuning or LLM prompt generation) and CLIP-AUTT for unsupervised, subject-level test-time personalization via entropy-guided temporal window selection combined with AU prompt tuning.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three distinct and challenging video ER datasets (BioVid, StressID, BAH) spanning controlled and in-the-wild conditions, with consistent gains over multiple recent CLIP-based FER and TTA baselines (TPT, TDA, DPE, PromptAlign, ReTA, T3AL).

Thorough ablation studies (temporal module design, prompt template choice, AU vs. class-prompt fusion, window-length sensitivity, robustness to random seeds, scalability with more target subjects, sentence- vs phrase-level AU prompts, an additional FERV39K generalization check) that substantively support the design choices.
Efficiency/complexity analysis (throughput, trainable parameters, GFLOPs) demonstrating the method is lightweight relative to full fine-tuning baselines, which is relevant for practical deployment.

Qualitative AU visualizations cross-checked against an independent AU detector (OpenFace) provide some external validation of the AU semantics the model learns, and the personalization concept is clearly illustrated with concrete subject examples.
weaknesses: No ground-truth AU annotations are used or evaluated quantitatively; the claim that CLIP-AUTT learns 'more meaningful' AU activations rests mainly on a handful of qualitative examples cross-checked against OpenFace, an imperfect detector itself — a quantitative AU-agreement metric (e.g., correlation with detector outputs across the full test set) would strengthen this central claim considerably.

On the most challenging dataset (BAH), CLIP-AUTT's UAR is essentially at chance level (~50.2%) and for several individual subjects UAR stays pinned at exactly 50.0, suggesting the method may be defaulting to majority-class-like behavior rather than achieving genuine class separation there, which tempers the personalization claims in real-world/in-the-wild conditions.

Test-time personalization pool is small (only 10 target subjects per dataset in the main results), and while a scalability plot up to 30 subjects is shown, subject-wise variance remains high (e.g., BioVid Sub-3 stuck at 50% WAR for all methods including CLIP-AUTT), limiting confidence in the generality of gains.

The core TTA mechanism (entropy minimization over a selected window with prompt tuning) is methodologically close to established TTA/prompt-tuning approaches (TENT, TPT, PromptAlign); the main novelty is the entropy-guided window selection and AU-specific prompting, which is a comparatively incremental technical contribution relative to the strong empirical claims made.

No comparison to existing supervised or source-free personalization/domain-adaptation methods for FER (e.g., MSDA/SFDA works cited in Related Work) is provided, despite personalization being a central theme; such baselines would better contextualize how much the AU-based text prompting itself (versus generic domain adaptation) contributes.

The fixed, hand-curated set of 46 AU prompts is not validated against dataset-specific facial behaviors or ablated in terms of AU selection/pruning, and it is unclear how sensitive results are to the exact wording/granularity of these AU phrases beyond the sentence-vs-phrase-level check.
